edges.why: Raising exactly the right number of fingers for each addend is counting out a set of a given number.
The total of all raised fingers is the sum, which is the meaning of joining two sets and counting all.
Step one counts the first run of sounds or actions as it happens, which is counting events.
Continuing the count from the kept last number through the second run is counting forward from a given number.
The last number said being the total of both runs uses the idea that the last word tells how many.
The start, joined and now amounts that are named in the telling are found by counting the cars.
Naming how many there are now after the joining is finding the total of the two sets by counting all.
The expression a + b stands for the start amount and the joined amount of a joining action told in words.
The expression is built from written numerals for the two amounts, so the learner must write numerals.
The equation a + b = c extends the expression a + b by recording the result of the same joining.
The equation also records the total c as a written numeral after the equal sign.
Raising fingers for the starting number is counting out a set of a given size on the fingers.
The fingers still raised are the difference, which is taking objects away and counting what is left.
The start, taken away and left amounts that the telling names are found by counting the birds.
Naming how many are left after the action is taking some away and counting what remains.
The expression a - b stands for the start amount and the amount taken away in a taking-away action told in words.
The expression is built from written numerals for the two amounts, so the learner must write numerals.
The equation a - b = c extends the expression a - b by recording what is left after the same taking away.
The equation also records the amount left c as a written numeral after the equal sign.
The learner makes a set of counters for each of the two parts, which is counting out a given number.
Finding the total of the two parts that are together is putting the sets together and counting all of them.
Step one makes a set with the given number of objects by counting them out.
Putting the set back together and splitting it again relies on the total staying the same when it is moved apart or together.
Drawing the two groups after separating the set is recording how many with marks or drawings.
The equation w = a + b records a split of w into two parts that the learner has already made.
The record a + b = w is the addition equation form for putting two amounts together to make a total.
Step one shows n objects, for example dots in a ten frame, by counting out n.
Adding objects one at a time until there are 10 is counting forward from n.
The partner is the number of objects added, which is found by counting those added objects.
Each item is presented as a written expression a + b whose meaning the learner must read.
The recalled sum is the same total that joining the two sets and counting all would give.
Each item is presented as a written expression a - b whose meaning the learner must read.
The recalled difference is the same amount left that taking away and counting what remains would give.
Saying the first addend and then continuing with the next number word is counting forward from a given number.
Stopping after exactly b words are counted on is the same control as counting out a set of a given number.
The last word said being the sum relies on the last number word telling how many in all.
The statement is about finding a + b, so the learner must know what the expression a + b stands for.
Saying the number one less each time is counting backward by ones.
Stopping after exactly b words are counted back is the same control as counting out a set of a given number.
The statement is about finding a - b, so the learner must know what the expression a - b stands for.
The statement a + b = b + a says the two sums have the same value, which is the meaning of the equal sign.
Both sides are written as sums a + b and b + a, so the learner reads the sum notation.
Joining the two amounts in either order gives one collection whose count does not depend on counting order.
Replacing a + b by b + a is allowed only because the order of the addends does not change the sum.
The statement's example is to count on from the larger addend after the switch, as in 2 + 9 becoming 9 + 2.
The task is a sum of three numbers written as an expression, which the learner must read.
The total of three collections is the same whichever two are counted together first, since a count does not depend on order.
Adding the third number to the first pair's sum, for example 3 + 10, can be done by counting on.
The test problem asks the learner to find the two numbers that make 10 before adding.
The statement a - b = c is a subtraction equation recording what is left after taking b from a.
The statement pairs it with the addition equation b + c = a, so the learner must read addition equations.
That c left after taking b from a means a splits into the parts b and c, recorded as a = b + c.
The difference a - b is the distance from b to a, which is the number that must be added to b to reach a.
Adding c to b is a jump of length c forward on the number line, ending at a.
The statement pairs the difference with the addition equation b + c = a, so the learner must read addition equations.
Step one rewrites a - b = ? as b + ? = a.
Step two finds the missing addend in an addition equation by a known fact or counting up.
The missing addend being the difference rests on a - b being the number that added to b makes a.
Step one finds the partner of a that makes 10, namely 10 - a.
Step two splits b into two parts, 10 - a and the rest, and records b as their sum.
The final sum 10 + the rest is a teen number written as 10 plus ones.
Each item is a written sum n + n whose meaning the learner must read.
The recalled double is the total of joining two equal sets and counting all of them.
Finding how much larger the other addend is, d, is finding the number that added to the smaller addend gives the larger.
Step two recalls the double a + a.
Step three adds the small amount d to the double, for example 12 + 1, by counting on.
Rewriting a + (a + d) as (a + a) + d is adding three numbers and choosing which two to add first.
Step one writes the teen number a as 10 plus its r ones.
Step two splits b into r and b - r and records b as their sum.
Subtracting the rest from 10 is taking objects away from a ten and finding what is left.
The statement is about a - b, so the learner must know what the expression a - b stands for.
The sums of two one-digit numbers that are 10 or less are part of this set and the pieces of the larger sums.
Sums greater than 10 are first reached by completing a ten and adding the rest, as in 8 + 5 = 10 + 3.
The differences within 10 are part of this set and are used for the last step across 10.
Differences that cross 10 are first reached by subtracting down to 10 and then the rest.
A difference such as 14 - 6 is reached by thinking of the addition 6 + ? = 14.
The thinking-addition route uses known sums of one-digit numbers, including those over 10.
The equal sign states that two numbers have the same value, as the = symbol does for whole-number comparisons.
Both sides in the examples are sums, so the learner must read an expression as standing for a value.
The test problem needs the values of 3 + 4 and 7 + 2 to see whether they are equal.
An equation is true when the two sides have the same value, which is the meaning of the equal sign.
Steps one and two find the value of a sum on either side.
Steps one and two find the value of a difference on either side.
Rewriting a - b = ? as b + ? = a is justified by the difference being the unknown addend.
The starting form a - b = ? is a subtraction equation with a symbol for the result.
The result b + ? = a is an addition equation with a symbol in the addend position.
The statement is about equations of the form a + b = c, so the learner must read addition equations.
Equations written either way round, such as 14 = 6 + ?, need the equal sign read as same value.
Finding the addend that added to a known addend makes the sum is done by counting up.
Step three checks that the two sides have equal values.
The statement is about equations of the form a - b = c, so the learner must read subtraction equations.
Equations written either way round, such as 5 = ? - 3, need the equal sign read as same value.
Finding an unknown difference, and the subtrahend a - c, is subtracting.
Finding the unknown minuend b + c is adding two known numbers.
The minuend being b + c follows from a difference being the unknown addend.
Step four checks that the two sides have equal values.
